leading_positions.synthesis: Six of eight members prefer the optical lattice clock (Katori and Ye) as a single-part prize; Eriksson, Johansson and Olsson say they moved to it after reading the opening ballots. Shared: the magic-wavelength idea, control of systematics to about 1e-18, independent reproduction in several laboratories, and a two-name attribution all supporters accept. Not shared: how much weight the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes carry, whether a precision-measurement invention counts as discovery, how to word the citation (clock itself versus applications), and how to treat early contributors outside the credited names (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and others). This is a count of explicit round-1 positions only.

Mehlig alone prefers the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class (Kardar and Zhang), citing a simple mechanism, exact one-dimensional results, Tracy-Widom statistics and liquid-crystal experiments. He presents it as a minority view and not a likely consensus, and keeps B030 and B058 as alternatives. Eriksson notes that Parisi, a 1986 co-author and 2021 laureate, is outside the credited names. Not shared: any other member's explicit preference for this candidate.

Danielsson alone prefers precision CMB anisotropy mapping (Bennett, Spergel, Puget), arguing maturity, independent confirmation and an open measurement side after COBE (2006) and the 2019 cosmology prize. He concedes that only he and the chair ranked it, calls the WMAP versus Planck and Page versus Puget allocation a real problem, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win. Olsson and Lindroth question whether a precision refinement of an already honoured discovery and an unsettled name set qualify.

areas_of_agreement: All seven members who comment on B030 agree on the scientific soundness of the optical lattice clock and on the pair Katori and Ye as the credited laureates; objections concern framing and overlap, not whether the physics is secure.

Several members (Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) say IceCube, topological insulators or the Higgs are scientifically strong but carry heavier attribution problems than the clock.
Members repeatedly say that a three-name limit makes any selection contestable for large-collaboration or multi-team candidates (B017, B020, B055).
Most members want expert reports on priority and credit questions before a final ballot, and the citation to be worded so that it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
scientific_disputes: Whether a precision-measurement invention such as the lattice clock is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, or an incremental refinement of work honoured in 2005 (comb) and 2012 (single quantum systems); Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Eriksson each raise some version of this.

How much of the clock's reach into fundamental physics (millimetre-scale redshift, constant variation, dark-matter searches, redefinition of the second) is demonstrated and how much is prospective; Olsson wants applications left out of the citation.

Whether IceCube's discovery of the diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux stands on its own (Pearce, Danielsson, Mehlig note it is confirmed in several channels) or depends on source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068), which Kroll and Johansson regard as still thin.

Whether topological insulators (B058) are a new class of matter distinct from the 2016 topology prize or a sequel, and how well HgTe edge conduction is quantized (Eriksson, Johansson, Olsson, Mehlig).

Whether precision CMB mapping (B055) is a new discovery or a refinement of the work behind the 2006 COBE prize (Olsson), against Danielsson's view that it established percent-level parameters not covered by COBE or the 2019 prize.
attribution_disputes: B030: the Katori and Ye pair is accepted by all proposers, but Kroll and Olsson ask how to split credit between Katori's proposal and first demonstration and Ye's 1e-18 and many-body results, and whether Lemonde's group and other early groups have a priority claim.

B055: proposals differ in the third name, Danielsson proposing Bennett, Spergel and Puget and Pearce proposing Bennett, Spergel and Page, which reflects an unresolved choice between WMAP and Planck and between analysis and instrument credit; Lindroth treats this as an unresolved name set.
B020: Halzen, Karle and Spiering are proposed by all five who ranked it, but Kroll, Olsson and Pearce ask how AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors and a collaboration of hundreds should be weighed.

B017: the four members who proposed laureates did not agree beyond Gianotti and Virdee; Jenni and Della Negra each appear on some ballots only, and Evans is left out, so the attribution is described as unresolved (Kroll, Olsson, Johansson, Mehlig).

B058: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp omit Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction) and the 3D contributors Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan; Olsson notes that Zhang has died (Eriksson, Mehlig, Kroll, Lindroth all raise the omissions).
B049: Kardar and Zhang omit Parisi, a 1986 co-author and 2021 laureate, and Spohn's later exact-solution work is a separate achievement (Mehlig, Eriksson).
B029: Wallraff, who performed the strong-coupling experiment, is not among the credited names (Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth).
maturity_disputes: The pending redefinition of the SI second: Johansson sees it as strengthening B030 and Kroll as making the recognition current, while Olsson and Pearce note the societal payoff is still prospective.
Whether IceCube is slightly early because source identification is incomplete (Kroll, Johansson) or mature because the diffuse flux is secure (Pearce, Danielsson, Mehlig).
Whether returning to superconducting circuits (B029) or to topology (B058) is too soon after the 2025 and 2016 prizes (Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson on B058).
Whether Cirac and Zoller (B044) can be framed as a theory prize distinct from the 2012 prize for the experiments (Johansson, Lindroth, Eriksson).
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson (Director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology) discloses a clear connection to B029 and a lesser one to B044, and says he would recuse or discount his own B029 ranking.

Olsson discloses a Fellowship at the University of Tokyo since 2025 and long-running exchanges there, where Katori is based, and flags it in case recusal on B030 is required; she reports no personal tie to Katori or Ye.

Kroll discloses a year in John Hall's laboratory at JILA, where Ye is based and previously worked in Hall's group, as a distant mentor-lineage link with no collaboration; he also leads WACQT and holds a stake in the spin-off Deep Light Vision, which he says is irrelevant to any candidate.
Pearce (chair) discloses field proximity to B020, as a Fermi-LAT member and in the neutrino-astronomy community, with no tie to credited individuals and no tie to Katori or Ye.
Lindroth discloses that she is close to the lattice-clock field and may be biased upward on B030, and a long collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, who is not credited on any shortlisted ballot.

Danielsson discloses a professional interest in dark-energy cosmology but no tie to Bennett, Spergel, Puget or Page; Eriksson (2025 Chair) and Mehlig (Chalmers environment alongside Johansson and Olsson) report no candidate-related conflicts.
questions_for_round2: Can the committee agree a citation for B030 that names the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realization, and separates it explicitly from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes?

Do expert reviewers find any priority claim (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or others) strong enough to change the two-name credit for Katori and Ye, and how should the share between Katori and Ye be described?

Does the committee accept a precision-measurement invention as discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and what weight should prospective uses such as the SI redefinition carry?

Do the minority proponents of B049 and B055 (Mehlig, Danielsson) still prefer them as first choice after reading B030 attribution arguments, or are they now content with B030 as the leading position, and what would change their rank?

Is there a defensible three-name rule for collaboration or multi-team candidates (B017, B020, B055) that the committee would accept, and can Danielsson and Pearce reconcile the Puget and Page trios for B055 if the candidate is kept alive?

If B030 leads, is any second part (for example B020 or B058) both distinct and fairly attributed within the three-person limit, as Pearce has not found a pairing that works, and do the others see one?
Does Olsson's Tokyo fellowship or Kroll's Hall-laboratory link require any recusal or discounting on B030, and does the committee want Johansson's B029 ranking discounted as he proposes?
summary.chair_observation: Round 1 shows a clear plurality position on B030 (six of eight explicit preferences) with agreed laureates, and two single-member minority positions on B049 and B055. The remaining disagreement is mostly about framing, overlap with earlier metrology prizes, and priority outside the credited names, while several scientifically strong alternatives remain blocked on attribution. The chair listed B020 first in the opening ballot and moved to B030 in round 1; this summary reports positions only and does not rule on any candidate.
